title: Fishers, a Leper, a Paralytic, and a Tax Collector
summary: After a miraculous catch of fish, Simon Peter falls at Jesus' knees confessing he is a sinful man, and he, James, and John leave everything to follow. Jesus touches and cleanses a leper, forgives and heals a paralyzed man lowered through a roof, and calls the tax collector Levi, whose banquet provokes a dispute with the Pharisees about eating with sinners and about fasting. Jesus answers with images of a bridegroom, new garments, and new wine.
story: Chapter 4 announced Jesus' mission and showed his authority over demons and disease. Now he begins to gather people around him, and the kinds of people he gathers are the point: fishermen who know they are sinful, a man whose disease has shut him out of community, a paralytic carried by friends, and a despised tax collector. The chapter also introduces the Pharisees and teachers of the law, who will watch and question him through the rest of the Gospel. The conflict begins not over politics but over forgiveness and table fellowship: who has the right to forgive sins, and whom God's messenger may eat with.
historical:
The Lake of Gennesaret is Luke's name for the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long, fed and drained by the Jordan. Fishing was a significant industry there, controlled by licenses and taxes under Herod Antipas, and fish were salted and exported. In 1986 a first-century fishing boat was found preserved in the mud of the lake's shore, giving a picture of the kind of vessel Peter and his partners worked from, about twenty-seven feet long.

The Pharisees appear here for the first time in Luke. They were a lay renewal movement within Judaism, respected by many ordinary people, who sought to apply the Law of Moses carefully to daily life, including rules of purity, tithing, and Sabbath, and who held to oral traditions that interpreted the written Law. Teachers of the law, or scribes, were experts trained in interpreting and applying Scripture; many were Pharisees. Levi collected tolls at a booth, probably at Capernaum on the road near the border between Antipas's and Philip's territories. Mark 2:14 also calls him Levi, while Matthew 9:9 names the same tax collector Matthew.
cultural:
What the Bible calls leprosy was not only what we now call Hansen's disease; the Hebrew and Greek terms covered a range of visible skin conditions described in Leviticus 13. The Law declared such a person ritually unclean, living apart from the community and warning others away. Touching him would, by ordinary understanding, have made Jesus unclean. Instead the cleansing flows the other way. Jesus sends the man to the priest with the offering prescribed in Leviticus 14, so that his restoration could be officially confirmed and he could return to worship and to his village.

Houses in the region were often built with flat roofs reached by outside stairs; Mark describes the men digging through the roof, while Luke speaks of tiles, the kind of roof his Greco-Roman readers would picture. Meals were more than food. To eat with someone was to accept them, and Pharisaic concern for purity made table company a serious matter. Fasting was a regular practice of devotion; Luke 18:12 has a Pharisee fasting twice a week. Wineskins were goat or sheep hides; new wine still fermenting would stretch and split an old, brittle skin.
literary: Luke assembles five scenes that belong together. The first, the call of the fishermen, is fuller than Mark 1:16-20 and Matthew 4:18-22, which simply record the call; its miraculous catch resembles the scene after the resurrection in John 21. The following four, the leper, the paralytic, Levi, and the fasting question, follow the order of Mark 1:40-2:22 and Matthew 8-9. The last three are controversy stories, in which an action of Jesus draws criticism and his answer ends in a memorable saying. Luke adds verse 39, found in no other Gospel, a wry comment that people who like the old wine do not want to try the new. Peter's reaction in verse 8 echoes Isaiah's in the temple (Isaiah 6:5): nearness to holiness exposes sin.

outline.t: The great catch and the call of the first disciples
Jesus touches and cleanses a leper
The paralyzed man forgiven and healed
Levi's call and banquet with tax collectors and sinners
The question about fasting: bridegroom, garments, and wineskins

doctrines.note: Jesus comes to call sinners to repentance, as a doctor comes to the sick. Salvation is not a prize for the healthy but healing for those who know they need it, as Peter does when he says he is a sinful man.

Forgiving sins was God's prerogative, as the scribes rightly note. Jesus claims that authority on earth. How he can offer forgiveness so freely will become clear only at the cross, where Luke shows him praying forgiveness for his executioners.
Jesus sees the faith of the friends who carried the paralyzed man. Faith in Luke is often persistent and practical, pushing through obstacles to get to Jesus.

words.note: Aphiemi, to release, let go, or forgive. It can mean leaving nets or canceling a debt. When Jesus says the paralytic's sins are forgiven, the verb pictures a debt released or a burden sent away. It is the verbal form of the noun for release in 4:18.

Hamartolos, sinner. Used of anyone who sins, but in Jesus' day it also labeled people seen as living outside the Law, such as tax collectors or those in dishonorable trades. Peter applies it to himself; the Pharisees apply it to others.

Katharizo, to cleanse or make clean. In the Greek Old Testament it describes ritual cleansing as well as physical healing. The leper asks to be made clean, not merely cured, because cleanness meant restoration to worship and community.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus doing what belongs to God. His word fills the nets where a night of skill had failed, and Peter's response, falling down and calling him Lord, is the response of a man before the holy God. He touches the unclean without becoming unclean. He forgives sins, and when the scribes object that only God can do so, he proves his authority by healing. He calls himself the Son of Man, a phrase from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man receives authority from God. And he calls himself the bridegroom, a role the Old Testament gives to God in his love for Israel (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2). His hint that the bridegroom will be taken away is the first quiet shadow of his death in Luke.

hard.q: Why does Jesus tell the healed leper not to tell anyone?
hard.a: Jesus often discourages publicity after healings, especially in Mark, and this command appears in several scenes. Several reasons have been suggested, and they are not exclusive. The practical one is that crowds seeking miracles made it hard for him to teach and move freely, as verse 15 shows happening anyway. A second is that popular hopes for a political or wonder-working Messiah could distort his mission, so he chose to reveal himself gradually, especially before the cross made plain what kind of Messiah he was. A third, in this case, is order: the man was first to go to the priest and be declared clean, completing the Law's process as a testimony, rather than spreading the news before his restoration was confirmed. Nineteenth and twentieth century scholars debated a so-called messianic secret as a literary theme of Mark; Luke keeps the command but places less emphasis on it.

questions: Peter responds to Jesus' power by saying, “Go away from me, Lord”. Why might closeness to God make a person more aware of their failings rather than less?
The paralyzed man got to Jesus because his friends carried him and broke through a roof. Who has carried you, or whom might you carry?
Jesus eats with people the respectable avoided. Whose table would he sit at in your town, and would you be comfortable there?
